To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the speed and accuracy of a BMI cursor can be controlled by the choice of Kalman filter parameters; 2) BMI cursor control is consistent with a feedforward control scheme; and 3) BMI control of redundant actuators is possible and can be achieved by exploiting the redundant control signals available to the BMI system

we have developed a novel method to extract sparse kinematic components from neural signals recorded during 2 D reaching movements and that we have shown how the speed accuracy trade off of BMI cursors can be manipulated through the use of Kalman filters.

1) we have developed a fast method for extracting sparse components of hand trajectory during reaching, 2) we discovered that BMI cursor control is model based, and 3) we demonstrated the use of redundant control signals in neuroprosthetic arm control.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design and development of control architectures for redundant neuroprosthesis systems.
the design and analysis of control algorithms to enable BMI control of highly complex and redundant robotic systems.
the development of control strategies for BMIs and the analysis of the neuroprosthetics control mechanisms used by subjects.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the work presented herein contributes to the development of BMI technology by providing new methods to analyze and design control systems that are more robust and more capable than current state of the art.
the work presented in this thesis contributes to the field of neuroprosthetic research in a number of important ways.
the work presented here has contributed to a deeper understanding of the neural basis of natural motor control and has developed a foundation for BMI control of redundant systems.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that the control of redundant multi DOF neuroprosthetic devices is possible, and we have identified several design considerations for the development of these systems.
BMI control of a virtual redundant arm can be performed by non human primate primates using neural signals recorded with implanted micro electrodes.
we have developed methods to improve BMI control performance and have begun to explore methods of redundant BMI control.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the design of neuroprosthetic systems must be carefully considered to ensure optimal performance.

the design of neuroprosthetic algorithms is a critical factor in determining the performance of the overall neuroprosthetic system, and the design of these algorithms must be guided by an understanding of the neurophysiology of natural motor control.
BMI systems can be designed to scale to redundant systems by incorporating redundancy into the neural decoding algorithms.
